47	Ideally, coalition members collectively identify and implement interventions with previously demonstrated potential to address local priorities effectively (Hawkins et al., 2008). Studies have found sustained improvements in youth outcomes to be associated with coalitions' use of evidence -based practices (EBPs) (Hawkins et al., 2014; Oesterle et al., 2018; Spoth et al., 2022). In practice, however, many coalitions do not select and implement such EBP (Gloppen et al., 2016). The community -based organizations involved in coalitions also often struggle to implement EBPs because of staf fi ng and funding constraints (Bach -Mortensen et al., 2018). Such constraints may also impede inclusive leadership, which requires substantial time, as well as the development of coalition leader skills. The current study focuses on how inclusive leadership, de fi ned as valuing members' distinctive perspectives and fostering a sense of belonging (Shore et al., 2011), affects coalition use of EBPs. Our overarching conceptualization derives from the Community Coalition Action Theory (Kegler & Swan, 2011) and related work by Brown et al. (2016), which draw on prior research and practice to describe how coalition functioning may affect program implementation and hence health outcomes. Key elements of coalition functioning noted in these frameworks include leadership, communication, and decision making, which are expected to affect member engagement, program planning and implementation, and hence community outcomes.
48	
49	In keeping with their breadth, Community Coalition Action Theory (Kegler & Swan, 2011) and Brown et al. (2016) do not provide speci fi c causal logic about how leadership may translate into more or less effective program selection and implementation. To clarify our predictions for the current study, we therefore also draw on the teams literature about how leadership affects decision quality and implementation. This is based on viewing coalitions as teams, that is, interdependent groups of people who communicate over time (Homans, 1958), and the premise that the social dynamics at the heart of teams are potentially applicable across a variety of settings.

The means for inclusive decision making and inclusion of community residents were 4.06 and 4.01 on a 1-5 scale. The number of EBPs reported ranged from 0 to 9. The range of EBP reach was 0 to 5370, but highly skewed, with a mean of 224. The average coalition service area included approximately 84,000 people. The majority of coalitions were in Pennsylvania (86%). Twenty-six (41%) of the 64 coalitions followed the Coalitions That Care model. The majority (64%) reported receiving external funding. Forty-one (64%) of the coalitions received TA. The average coalition size was 36 members. After controlling for covariates and the initial value of each outcome, engaging communication and inclusive decision making showed significant associations (p<.05) with the number of EBPs a year later. Inclusion of community residents was positively associated with number of EBPs, but the association was only marginally significant, at p=.07 (Table 2). Each of these inclusive leadership practices was also shown to have significant positive associations (p<.05 in each case) with the reach of coalitions' evidence-based practices a year later (Table 3). In contrast, none of the inclusive leadership practices that we examined was associated with subsequent EBP fidelity (Table 4). In the fully adjusted lagged models for the number of EBPs and EBP fidelity, none of the covariates remained significant. However, in the models for EBP reach, following the CTC model was significant (p<.01) when the predictor was engaging in communication or inclusive decision making. Being externally funded was also associated with EBP reach (p<.05) when inclusive decision making was the primary independent variable. Cronbach's alpha = 0.93. Verifying that 1108/1851 rounds to 60% requires a division, which no available tool performs on this input form; grim_percentage would only confirm that 60% is attainable at n=1851, which at that sample size is uninformative (granularity ~0.05%). Recording the division as a hand calculation would breach the no-hand-arithmetic rule, so it was left unchecked.

unchecked.location: Supporting Information S1: Tables S1 and S2 (registry hierarchy used to classify programs as EBPs)
unchecked.reason: Supplementary file not provided with the paper; its contents could not be read or checked. The EBP classification rule -- and the noted 'discrepancies across registries, albeit few' -- underpins the paper's primary outcome and is not verifiable from what was supplied.

unchecked.location: Sensitivity analyses omitting coalitions with no EBPs
unchecked.reason: The paper states 'Sensitivity analyses omitting these coalitions yielded very similar associations to those reported here' but reports no coefficients, standard errors or p-values from them. There is nothing numeric to check.

unchecked.location: Confidence intervals for every coefficient in Tables 2-4
unchecked.reason: None are reported anywhere in the paper, so check_estimate_ci could not be run on any of the 63 coefficients -- normally the highest-yield check on a regression paper. Deriving intervals from the coefficients and standard errors would have required hand arithmetic and was not done.

The paper contains no data figures. The markdown extraction shows only decorative/logo image placeholders, and extract_pdf surfaced no figure captions carrying statistics. No figure-derived values were used anywhere in this sweep.

unchecked.location: Coalition service area population, community poverty, coalition age and state as candidate covariates
unchecked.reason: These are named in the Covariates section as having been screened for inclusion, but the bivariate screening results (p-values, associations) are never reported -- only the final retained set. The screening tests that led to their exclusion cannot be checked, which also means the multiplicity implied by that screening cannot be quantified.
